posts.title: Before you argue the point, ask who decides it.
posts.caption: Before you argue the point, ask who decides it. Most fights in a meeting are not about the idea. They are about talking to the wrong room. The people nodding cannot say yes, and the person who can say yes is not in the room. So ask early, and ask plainly. Who makes this call? Who signs it? Who can stop it? When you know the decider, you stop performing for the crowd and start making the case to the one person who matters. Find the decider first. Then argue. Full breakdown in the 209connect newsletter, link in bio.

posts.title: Every request needs a date, or it is not a request.
posts.caption: Every request needs a date, or it is not a request. It is a wish. 'I'll get back to you' means nothing until a day is attached to it. So ask for the date, every time. When someone says soon, ask what day. A promise with no date has no owner and no ending, and it drifts until everyone forgets it was made. A date turns a promise into a plan. It gives the work a finish line and gives you something real to check. Stop accepting someday. Ask for the date, write it down, and hold the line when it comes. Full breakdown in the 209connect newsletter, link in bio.

posts.title: West Sacramento's Mayor Said It Out Loud: ICE Is Not Welcome Here
posts.caption:
Central Valley governance. Merced County spending. Administrative accountability.

Here is what West Sacramento just showed us about how local government actually works. The mayor and a council member did not wait for a federal agency to ask permission. They told residents ICE is not welcome, and they named where to report it: NorCal Resist. The city passed a resolution in May that keeps city resources out of federal immigration enforcement. And the mayor says four people have been detained in the city in the past two weeks. The lesson: a resolution on paper only matters if the people who passed it say it out loud.

New story every day. Deep dives in the 209connect newsletter, link in bio, free.

posts.title: California, Explained: Closed Session.
posts.caption:
California, Explained: Closed Session. Closed session is not a secret meeting. It is a narrow exception, and the law lists exactly what fits inside: personnel, litigation, labor talks, and real property negotiations. Everything else belongs in public, with an agenda, in the open. When a board goes behind closed doors, the agenda has to say why. No reason listed means no closed session. Read the agenda before the meeting, check the exception, and if the reason is not on the list, say so.

posts.title: California, Explained: LCFF, the formula that pays for your schools.
posts.caption:
California, Explained: LCFF, the formula that pays for your schools. Since 2013, California has funded schools with the Local Control Funding Formula. Every district gets a base amount for every student, and then extra money follows the students who need more support: English learners, foster youth, and students from low-income families. The neediest districts get more still. And every district must write a public plan, the LCAP, showing how that money follows the students it is meant for. The formula is the promise. The plan is the receipt. Read the plan, and see whether the money went where the law said it should.

posts.caption:

posts.title: Who watches the county government when nobody is watching? In Merced County, the answer is nineteen
posts.caption:
Who watches the county government when nobody is watching? In Merced County, the answer is nineteen ordinary citizens. The civil grand jury serves a one-year term starting January first, and the foreperson is appointed by the grand jury judge. They split into committees and investigate county departments, cities, and special districts. Any citizen can file a complaint, and that complaint can trigger an investigation. Twice a year they publish reports with findings and recommendations, and the agencies they investigate have to answer in writing. It is the one watchdog in county government that answers to no politician, only to the California Constitution. California, Explained.
